summary: Lists the DHCP options that carry extra settings to clients, along with the BOOTP vendor extensions they build on. It was replaced by RFC 2132.

eli5.summary: DHCP can hand a computer a pile of small notes with answers like which router and which name server to use. This memo lists the notes.

questions: dhcp options and bootp vendor extensions
what is the dhcp magic cookie
what is the difference between bootp vendor extensions and dhcp options
subtitle: The list of tagged settings that DHCP and BOOTP can hand to a host, from subnet mask to NTP servers.

tldr.problem: DHCP and BOOTP need a common, extensible way to pass configuration data such as addresses of routers and servers to a booting host.
tldr.mechanism: Each setting is a tagged option made of a code octet, a length octet and data, stored in the options field of the message. The RFC lists the codes 0 to 61, including those from RFC 1497 and the ones used only by DHCP.
tldr.outcome: It was the option list of its time and was obsoleted by RFC 2132, which carries a new, complete list.

today: RFC 1533 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2132, which carries the later full list of DHCP options. It replaced the earlier BOOTP vendor extension documents, including RFC 1497.

sections.title: What This Document Defines
sections.content:
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) passes configuration parameters to hosts on a TCP/IP network. Those parameters are carried as tagged data items, called options, in the options field of the DHCP message. RFC 1533 specifies the current set of DHCP options, and says each superseding document will include the entire current list.

It also folds in the BOOTP vendor information extensions of RFC 1497, which it supersedes. Every option here, except the ones specific to DHCP in section 9, may also be used as a BOOTP vendor extension. The document obsoletes RFCs 1497, 1395, 1084 and 1048.
sections.eli5: DHCP can give a new computer many small answers to questions it would otherwise have to guess. This memo is the dictionary of what those answers can be.

sections.title: How an Option Is Encoded
sections.content:
Every option starts with a tag octet that identifies it. Only options 0 (pad) and 255 (end) are a single octet. All others have a length octet after the tag, and the length does not count the tag and length octets themselves. Multi-octet values are in network byte order.

When used with BOOTP, the first four octets of the vendor field hold a magic cookie: the value 99.130.83.99, which is hexadecimal 63.82.53.63. Pad can align fields, and end marks the end of valid information, with later octets filled with pad.

Option codes 128 to 254 are reserved for site-specific options. New options defined after this document should carry a length octet even if the length is fixed or zero. Additional generic option codes are registered through IANA, and using undefined codes in the range 61 to 127 may conflict with other implementations.
sections.eli5: Each note has a label number, then a size, then the stuff. It is like a luggage tag, a weight and the bag itself.

sections.title: The Vendor Extensions Carried Over from RFC 1497
sections.content:
Section 3 repeats the extensions from RFC 1497, so that the list is complete. The most used ones tell the client about its network:

  • Subnet Mask (code 1), 4 octets. If it appears with the router option in a DHCP reply, it MUST come first.
  • Time Offset (2), a signed 32-bit offset in seconds from UTC.
  • Router (3), a list of router addresses in order of preference; the length is a multiple of 4.
  • Time Server (4), Name Server (5), Domain Name Server (6), Log Server (7), Cookie Server (8), LPR Server (9), Impress Server (10) and Resource Location Server (11), each a list of addresses.
  • Host Name (12), Boot File Size (13), Merit Dump File (14), Domain Name (15), Swap Server (16), Root Path (17) and Extensions Path (18).

The server lists use a common layout of a code, a length n, and one or more 4-octet IP addresses, which SHOULD be in order of preference.
sections.eli5: The first group of notes tells a computer the basics: its network size, the way out (the router), who to ask for names, and what its own name is.

sections.title: IP, Link, TCP and Application Parameters
sections.content:
The new options in sections 4 to 8 tune the host's network stack and point it at services. They are grouped as follows.

  • IP layer, per host (19 to 25): IP forwarding on or off, non-local source routing, policy filters, maximum datagram reassembly size (minimum 576), default IP time-to-live, and Path MTU aging timeout and plateau table.
  • IP layer, per interface (26 to 33): interface MTU (minimum legal value 68), all-subnets-local, broadcast address, mask discovery and mask supplier, router discovery and the router solicitation address, and static routes. The default route 0.0.0.0 is an illegal destination for a static route.
  • Link layer (34 to 36): trailer encapsulation, ARP cache timeout, and Ethernet encapsulation.
  • TCP (37 to 39): default TTL, keepalive interval, and the keepalive garbage octet.
  • Applications and services (40 to 49): NIS domain and servers, NTP servers, vendor-specific information, NetBIOS name and datagram servers, node type and scope, and X Window System font servers and display managers.

Option 43, vendor-specific information, is an opaque object. A vendor that encodes several items SHOULD use encapsulated options with the same code, length and value syntax, but without a magic cookie. Servers that cannot interpret it MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: More notes let the network fine-tune the computer, such as how big its packets can be, how long to wait before checking a connection, and where to find the printer or the clock.

sections.title: Options Used Only by DHCP
sections.content:
Section 9 defines options that exist only in DHCP and cannot be used as BOOTP extensions. The client and server use them to run the address lease.

  • Requested IP Address (50) and IP Address Lease Time (51, in seconds as a 32-bit unsigned integer).
  • Option Overload (52): value 1 means the file field holds options, 2 means the sname field does, and 3 means both.
  • DHCP Message Type (53), with values 1 to 7 for DHCPDISCOVER through DHCPRELEASE.
  • Server Identifier (54), the IP address of the selected server. Servers put it in a DHCPOFFER so the client can tell offers apart, and the client includes it in a DHCPREQUEST to say which offer it accepts.
  • Parameter Request List (55), where the client lists the option codes it wants; the server MUST try to return them in the requested order.
  • Message (56) for error text, Maximum DHCP Message Size (57, minimum legal value 576), Renewal T1 (58) and Rebinding T2 (59) times, Class-identifier (60) and Client-identifier (61).

The Client-identifier is how DHCP servers index their database of address bindings, and it is expected to be unique in an administrative domain. It typically contains a hardware type and hardware address, but this is not required.
sections.eli5: A few notes only DHCP uses: asking for a particular address, saying how long you may keep it, and saying whether this message is a hello, an offer, a yes or a no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of RFC 1533 consists of a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The options it defines carry configuration such as routers, name servers and time servers, but the RFC does not analyze what happens if they are forged.
sections.eli5: This memo does not talk about how to stop someone from handing out fake notes.
